The Populist Party, also known as the People's Party. It emerged in the 1890s as a radical agrarian and labor movement responding to rural hardship, farm debt, and industrial monopolies.

The party arose from the Farmers' Alliance movement. It championed debt-ridden farmers in the South and Great Plains who blamed railroads, banks, and urban elites for their plight. In the 1892 presidential election, Populist candidate James Weaver won over 8 percent of the popular vote and 22 electoral votes. This was the strongest showing for a third party since the Republican Party's founding in 1856.

The party demanded unlimited coinage of silver at a ratio of 16 to 1 with gold—what they called free silver. They believed this inflation would ease farm debt and aid debtors over creditors. Populist platforms also included government ownership of railroads and telegraph lines, an eight-hour workday, and restrictions on land ownership by foreign investors.

Then came the 1896 presidential election. William Jennings Bryan, the Democratic nominee, adopted the Populist free-silver plank and famously proclaimed that the cross of gold would not be used to crucify mankind. This effectively ended the Populist Party as an independent force, though some continued calling themselves Populists into the early 1900s. Bryan's capture of the Democratic nomination meant the party's political energy was absorbed into the broader Democratic movement.

Many of the Populist ideas became mainstream Democratic policy: railroad regulation, antitrust action, and labor protections all bore the party's imprint on American political life.
